newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Malaysia Air results beat forecast.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Malaysia Air results beat forecast.

text.p: Malaysia Airline System Bhd on Thursday reported net earnings of 332.86 million ringgit ($132.6 million) for its 1996/97 financial year, exceeding analysts' projections
The 39.1 percent increase on last year's profits was above market forecasts, and pointed to a variety of factors which could have boosted profits, including two aircraft sales, analysts said.
"We were looking at around 270 (million ringgit), and it's slightly above our expectations," said Choo Swee Kee, airline analyst at Vickers Ballas.
The national carrier, better known as MAS, said its pretax profit was 349.41 million ringgit on a turnover of 6.48 billion ringgit for the year ended March 31, 1997.
"The results would have been better if not for higher fuel prices and the outbreak of cholera in Penang resulting in passenger cancellations," the company said in a statement.
It said yields remained under pressure due to excess capacity and keen competition but was positive on its move to the new Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Sepang.
The move "will provide greater opportunities for expansion of the company's operations", MAS said.
The Edinburgh Financial Publishing's Estimate Directory, which polled 31 analysts covering the stock, projected net profit to be 261 million ringgit if aircraft sales were not included.

The company said it sold two B-737-400 aircraft during the financial year for a gain of 43.8 million ringgit. "It's in line with my forecast and...above market expectations in the Estimate Directory," said Shamsul Shamsuddin, aviation analyst at Pesaka Jardine Fleming. "I was expecting around 280 million (ringgit) and the market 252.2 million. So leaving out the aircraft sales of around 44 million, it tallies."
"From the very basic numbers, it appears that they have benefited from a long-term, fuel-cost arrangement with Petronas," she added.
Ongoing cost-cutting measures by MAS chairman Tajudin Ramli were mentioned as another factor for the much-improved bottom line.

Said Sebastian Chang, research manager at Mohaiyani Securities: "Jet fuel costs went up an average 19 percent year-on-year in 1996. I think the full impact of their cost-cutting exercise has taken place."
